'''Oktay Sinanoğlu''' (February 25, 1935 – April 19, 2015) was a [[Turkish people|Turkish]] [[physical chemistry|physical chemist]] and [[molecular biophysics|molecular biophysicist]] who made contributions to the theory of [[electron correlation]] in molecules, the [[statistical mechanics]] of [[Clathrate hydrate|clathrate hydrates]], [[quantum chemistry]], and the theory of [[solvation]].

==Early life and education==
Sinanoğlu was born in [[Bari, Italy]] on February 25, 1935. His parents were Rüveyde (Karacabey) Sinanoğlu and Nüzhet Haşim. His father Rüveyde was a writer, and a consular official in the Bari consulate of [[Turkey]].<ref name="rg1"/> Following his father's recall to Turkey in July 1938, the family returned to Turkey before the start of [[World War II]].<ref name="rg2"/><ref name="yn1"/> He had a sister, [[Esin Afşar]] (1936-2011), who became a well-known singer and actress.<ref name="s1"/>

Sinanoğlu graduated from [[TED Ankara Koleji]] in 1951. He went to the United States in 1953, where he studied in [[University of California, Berkeley]]  graduating with a BSc degree in 1956. The following year, he completed an MSc degree at [[MIT]] (1957), and was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]]. He completed a [[predoctoral fellow]]ship (1958-1959) and earned his PhD in physical chemistry (1959-1960) at the University of California, Berkeley, advised by [[Kenneth Pitzer]].<ref name="yn1"/><ref name="s1"/><ref name="nyt1"/>

== Academic career ==
In 1960, Sinanoğlu joined the chemistry department at [[Yale University]].  He was appointed full professor of chemistry in 1963.<ref name="ydn1"/>  At age 28, he became the youngest full professor in Yale’s 20th-century history. It has been claimed that he was also the third-youngest full professor in the 300-plus year history of Yale University.<ref name="yn1"/>

During his tenure at Yale he wrote a number of papers in various subfields of theoretical chemistry, the most widely cited of which was his 1961 paper on electron correlation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sinanoğlu |first1=Oktay |title=Many-Electron Theory of Atoms and Molecules |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA |date=August 1961 |volume=47 |issue=8 |pages=1217–1226 |doi=10.1073/pnas.47.8.1217 |pmid=16590874 |pmc=223126 |bibcode=1961PNAS...47.1217S |doi-access=free }}</ref> This work anticipated the widely used [[coupled cluster]] method for describing electrons in molecules with greater accuracy than is possible via the [[Hartree–Fock method|Hartree-Fock method]]. He also published notable papers on the statistical mechanics of clathrate hydrates,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McKoy |first1=V. |last2=Sinanoğlu |first2=O. |date=1963-06-15 |title=Theory of Dissociation Pressures of Some Gas Hydrates |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1733625 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=38 |issue=12 |pages=2946–2956 |doi=10.1063/1.1733625 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c00494 |pmid=33226781 |s2cid=227159864 |issn=0009-2665|url-access=subscription }}</ref> solvation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sinano?lu |first=Oktay |date=August 1980 |issn=0020-7608|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stefaniuk |first1=Anna |last2=Gawinkowski |first2=Sylwester |last3=Golec |first3=Barbara |last4=Gorski |first4=Aleksander a method for predicting energy level patterns for compounds from the manipulation of graphs.<ref name="Oktay"/> He intended for chemists to be able to use the VIF method to predict the ways in which (Hydrides of Main Group Elements, Radicals, Cations, Anions) and MO Energy Level Patterns Directly from the Pictorial "VIF" Method Compared with Computer Calculations |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/j100074a010 |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry |language=en |volume=98 |issue=23 |pages=5867–5877 |doi=10.1021/j100074a010 |issn=0022-3654|url-access=subscription }}</ref>   After 37 years on the Yale faculty, Sinanoğlu retired in 1997.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hughes |first1=Sally Smith |url=https://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/rohoia/ucb/text/chemistadmin00pitzrich.pdf |title=Kenneth Sanborn Pitzer, Chemist and Administrator at UC Berkeley, Rice University, Stanford University, and the Atomic Energy Commission, 1935-1997, An oral history conducted in 1996-1998 |last2=LaBerge |first2=Germaine |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |year=1999 |location=The Bancroft Library |pages=135–136}}</ref>

During his time at Yale, Sinanoğlu served as a consultant to  Turkish universities, the [[Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey]] (TÜBİTAK), and the [[Japan Society for the Promotion of Science]] (JSPS).<ref name="yn1"/> In 1962, the Board of Trustees of [[Middle East Technical University]] in Ankara granted him the title of "consulting professor."<ref name="s1"/>

After his retirement from Yale, Sinanoğlu was appointed to the chemistry department of [[Yıldız Technical University]] in Istanbul, serving until 2002.<ref name="hdn1"/>

Sinanoğlu was the author or co-author of over 200 scientific articles and books. He also authored books on contemporary affairs in Turkey and [[Turkish language]], such as "Target Turkey" and "Bye Bye Turkish" (2005).<ref name="yn1"/><ref name="hdn1"/> In "Bye Bye Turkish", he propounded the [[Pseudoscientific language comparison|idea]] of cognation between Turkish and Japanese based on the alleged similarity of a number of words.

A 2001 best-seller book about his life and works, edited by Turkish writer [[Emine Çaykara]], referred to him as "The Turkish Einstein, Oktay Sinanoğlu" ({{langx|tr|Türk Aynştaynı Oktay Sinanoğlu Kitabı}}).<ref name="yn1"/><ref name="os"/>

== Honors ==
He received the "TÜBİTAK Science Award" for chemistry in 1966,<ref name="tübitak"/> the [[Humboldt Prize#Past winners|Alexander von Humboldt Research Award]] in chemistry in 1973, and the "International Outstanding Scientist Award of Japan" in 1975. It has been reported in Turkish media that Sinanoğlu was a two-time nominee for the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]],<ref name="hdn1"/> but this claim is not supported by actual data from the Nobel Foundation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.malumatfurus.org/oktay-sinanoglunun-nobel-odulune-2-kez-aday-oldugu-ve-nobel-odulunu-reddettigi-iddiasi/ |title=Oktay Sinanoğlu'nun Nobel Ödülüne 2 Kez Aday Olduğu ve Nobel Ödülünü Reddettiği İddiası | language=tr |access-date=29 August 2023 |date=15 August 2019 | publisher=Malumatfuruş}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
On December 21, 1963, Oktay Sinanoğlu married Paula Armbruster,<ref name="m"/> who was doing graduate work at Yale University. The wedding ceremony took place in the [[Branford College]] Chapel of Yale.<ref name="nyt1"/> They had three children. After their later divorce, he married Dilek Sinanoğlu and from this marriage he became the father of twins. The family resided in the Emerald Lakes neighborhood of [[Fort Lauderdale]], [[Florida]], and in [[Istanbul]], Turkey.<ref name="yn1"/>

Dilek Sinanoğlu made public on April 10, 2015, that Oktay Sinanoğlu was hospitalized in [[Miami]], [[Florida]], and was in a coma in the intensive care unit.<ref name="h1"/>  He died at age 80 on April 19, 2015. No medical statement was released about the cause of the death.<ref name="aa1"/> His body was transferred to Turkey, where he was buried in [[Karacaahmet Cemetery]], [[Üsküdar]] following the religious funeral service at [[Şakirin Mosque]].<ref name="h2" />
